title: Volunteers Wanted: Play Hide-and-Seek With the TSA's Sniffer Dogs
summary:
Want to play hide-and-seek with a dog at the airport — and help keep travellers safe? The Transportation Security Administration, or TSA, is looking for volunteers to do just that.

The volunteers act as decoys for the TSA's explosive detection dogs. In the TSA's words, they play a 'covert role player' — a pretend passenger who carries a 'training item' while wandering through the airport. You might wait in the ticketing lobby, go through security, or sit near a gate as if you were waiting for a flight. Then the dog team gets to work, trying to sniff you out.

The TSA says a shift 'may feel like a high-stakes game of hide and seek.' It is a game with a serious purpose: the training is an important part of keeping the dog teams ready for duty. The whole set-up is meant to copy what the dogs might face in the real world, so they are sharp when it matters.

A volunteer shift takes about two to three hours. You need to be at least 18 years old to sign up on your own, although younger volunteers can take part alongside an adult companion, in limited ways. You also need to be comfortable sitting, walking and moving around an airport — and wheelchair and scooter users can take part in the programme too.

If you love dogs, there is an extra treat in store. The TSA's annual calendar will be available in December, and it features the agency's working dogs. This year's star is Bolt, a German shorthaired pointer who won the TSA's Cutest Canine Contest for 2026. Bolt will be one of the dogs pictured on the 2027 calendar.

So if you have a free afternoon and a love of dogs, this might be the volunteer job for you.
why_it_matters: Sniffer dogs help keep airports safe for everyone who flies, and the training shows how volunteers and working animals can work together to protect travellers.

background_read: The TSA is the agency that keeps air travel in the United States safe, and its officers check passengers and bags at airports.
Some of its working dogs are trained to sniff out explosives, and they need regular practice to stay good at their job.
In training, volunteers pretend to be ordinary passengers so the dogs can practise finding them in real airport places like lobbies and gates.
The dogs work in teams with their handlers, and the practice helps the teams stay ready for real duty.
